item.title: The Body and Business Ethics
item.content:encoded:
Ajnesh Prasad, Audencia Business School

Eric Li, University of British Columbia

Natalia Vershinina, Audencia Business School

Alejandro Centeno, American University of Beirut

This special issue examines the intersection of embodiment and business ethics within organizational contexts. The call addresses how bodies are shaped by and through work, labor, and market systems, exploring the ethical implications of emotional labor, physical strain, commodification, and disciplinary practices. It seeks to move business ethics beyond abstract and conceptual frameworks toward understanding how embodied experiences and corporeal practices generate ethical dilemmas in organizational life.

The special issue welcomes diverse methodological approaches to investigating embodied labor across various industries including modeling, sports, healthcare, and entertainment. Contributions should interrogate how organizational norms regulate bodies in ways that reflect broader inequalities related to gender, race, and class, while also considering worker resistance and alternative theoretical frameworks such as feminist ethics and affect theory that center the lived body in ethical analysis.

Appel publié par Journal of Business Ethics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Ethical dimensions of emotional and relational labor through embodied experience
  • The ethics of body commodification in market-driven labor contexts
  • The embodied toll of labor and the ethical responsibilities of organizations
  • The gendered, racialized, and classed regulation of bodies in organizations
  • Participatory, sensory, or arts-based methods to research embodiment and ethics
  • New theoretical perspectives on embodiment in business ethics

Timeline

item.title: Ethics and Entrepreneurship: Foundations and Philosophical Perspectives
item.content:encoded:
Tina Dacin, Wilfrid Laurier University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Jean Clarke, Emlyon Business School

Jaco Lok, Macquarie University

Max Ganzin, Macquarie University

This special issue examines the ethical foundations of entrepreneurship, positioning ethics as central to entrepreneurial practice rather than a constraint on it. The issue brings together entrepreneurship studies and philosophical ethics to explore how venture creation, opportunity recognition, and stakeholder engagement involve fundamental questions about responsibility, justice, and human flourishing. It investigates the tension between entrepreneurship's capacity for creativity and disruption and concerns about commodification and self-optimization.

The special issue welcomes diverse methodological and disciplinary perspectives examining how philosophical traditions such as virtue ethics, phenomenology, pragmatism, and deontology illuminate entrepreneurial practice. It particularly emphasizes entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty and fluidity, where ethical judgment must balance competing stakeholder interests without reliance on established protocols. The issue seeks papers exploring how entrepreneurship and ethics can deepen each other's understanding through examining contingency, creativity, authenticity, care, and emerging futures.

Appel publié par Journal of Business Ethics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Philosophical dimensions of ethics and how different philosophical traditions inform understanding of entrepreneurship as an ethical practice
  • Phenomenology of the entrepreneurial experience, uncertainty, autonomy, and decision-making
  • The entrepreneur and ethical subjectivity, agency, embodiment, and identity
  • Ethics and rule-breaking in entrepreneurial contexts
  • Stakeholder relations, trust-building, and ethical objectives
  • Whether entrepreneurship is inherently ethical or exploitative
  • Entrepreneurship and technological mediation in the digital age
  • Ethics, value, and the framing of entrepreneurial goals and opportunities
  • Temporal dimensions of entrepreneurial ethics and long-term considerations

Timeline
